theory.title: Closures & Lexical Scope
theory.content:
What Is Lexical Scope?

JavaScript uses lexical (static) scoping — the scope of a variable is determined by where it is written in the source code, not where it is called from. When the engine resolves a name, it walks outward through the enclosing scopes at definition time.

function outer() {
  const message = 'hello';
  function inner() {
    console.log(message); // 'hello' — captured from outer scope
  }
  return inner;
}
const fn = outer();
fn(); // 'hello' — outer() has returned, but message lives on

What Is a Closure?

A closure is the combination of a function and the lexical environment in which it was declared. Closures allow functions to access variables from an outer scope even after that outer function has returned.

function createCounter(start = 0) {
  let count = start; // private — not accessible from outside
  return {
    increment() { return ++count; },
    decrement() { return --count; },
    value() { return count; }
  };
}
const counter = createCounter(10);
counter.increment(); // 11
counter.increment(); // 12
counter.value();     // 12

Common Use Cases

  • Data encapsulation — hide implementation details, expose only an API
  • Factory functions — create specialised functions with baked-in config
  • Memoization — cache expensive results using a closure-held Map
  • Partial application / currying — fix some arguments, return a new function

Classic Pitfall: Loop Variables

// BUG — all callbacks share the same `i` (var has function scope)
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0); // prints 3 3 3
}

// FIX 1 — use let (block scope creates a new binding per iteration)
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0); // prints 0 1 2
}

// FIX 2 — IIFE to capture current value
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  (function(j) {
    setTimeout(() => console.log(j), 0);
  })(i);
}

theory.title: Prototype Chain & Inheritance
theory.content:
Prototype-Based Inheritance

Every JavaScript object has an internal [[Prototype]] slot pointing to another object (or null). When you access a property that doesn't exist on the object itself, the engine traverses the prototype chain upward until it finds it or reaches null.

const animal = {
  breathe() { return `${this.name} breathes`; }
};

const dog = Object.create(animal); // dog.__proto__ === animal
dog.name = 'Rex';

dog.breathe(); // 'Rex breathes' — found on prototype
Object.getPrototypeOf(dog) === animal; // true

Constructor Functions

Before ES6 classes, constructors + prototype were the standard pattern:

function Person(name, age) {
  this.name = name;
  this.age = age;
}
Person.prototype.greet = function() {
  return `Hi, I'm ${this.name}`;
};

const alice = new Person('Alice', 30);
alice.greet(); // 'Hi, I'm Alice'
alice instanceof Person; // true

ES6 Classes (Syntactic Sugar)

Classes are a cleaner syntax over the same prototype mechanics:

class Animal {
  constructor(name) { this.name = name; }
  speak() { return `${this.name} makes a sound`; }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
  speak() { return `${this.name} barks`; }
  fetch(item) {
    return `${super.speak()} and fetches ${item}`;
  }
}

const rex = new Dog('Rex');
rex.speak(); // 'Rex barks'
rex instanceof Animal; // true — prototype chain intact

Key Methods

  • Object.create(proto) — create object with explicit prototype
  • Object.getPrototypeOf(obj) — read prototype
  • Object.setPrototypeOf(obj, proto) — change prototype (avoid in hot paths)
  • hasOwnProperty(key) — check own vs inherited property

theory.title: Event Loop & Async Execution
theory.content:
The Single-Thread Model

JavaScript runs in a single thread — only one piece of code executes at a time. The event loop coordinates how synchronous code, microtasks, and macrotasks are scheduled.

Execution Order

  1. Run all synchronous code (call stack)
  2. Process all microtasks (Promise callbacks, queueMicrotask)
  3. Run one macrotask (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O)
  4. Process all new microtasks again
  5. Repeat
console.log('1 — sync');

setTimeout(() => console.log('4 — macrotask'), 0);

Promise.resolve()
  .then(() => console.log('3 — microtask 1'))
  .then(() => console.log('3b — microtask 2'));

console.log('2 — sync');

// Output: 1 → 2 → 3 → 3b → 4

Microtasks vs Macrotasks

  • Microtasks: Promise .then/.catch/.finally, queueMicrotask(), MutationObserver
  • Macrotasks: setTimeout, setInterval, setImmediate (Node), I/O callbacks, requestAnimationFrame

Practical Impact

// Never starve the event loop with infinite microtasks
function recursiveMicrotask() {
  Promise.resolve().then(recursiveMicrotask); // blocks macrotasks forever!
}

// Prefer scheduling with setTimeout for long-running tasks
function processChunk(items, index = 0) {
  if (index >= items.length) return;
  processItem(items[index]);
  setTimeout(() => processChunk(items, index + 1), 0); // yields to event loop
}

theory.title: Promises & Async/Await
theory.content:
Promise States

A Promise is an object representing an eventual value. It moves through three states: pending → fulfilled (resolved) or rejected. Once settled, it never changes state.

const p = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  setTimeout(() => resolve('done'), 1000);
});

p.then(value => console.log(value))  // 'done' after 1s
 .catch(err => console.error(err))
 .finally(() => console.log('cleanup'));

Promise Chaining

Each .then() returns a new Promise, enabling clean sequential async operations:

fetch('/api/user/1')
  .then(res => res.json())
  .then(user => fetch(`/api/posts?userId=${user.id}`))
  .then(res => res.json())
  .then(posts => console.log(posts))
  .catch(err => console.error('Pipeline failed:', err));

Async/Await

async/await is syntactic sugar over Promises. An async function always returns a Promise. await pauses execution inside the function until the Promise settles.

async function loadUserData(userId) {
  try {
    const res = await fetch(`/api/users/${userId}`);
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
    const user = await res.json();
    return user;
  } catch (err) {
    console.error('Failed to load user:', err);
    throw err; // re-throw so callers can handle it
  }
}

Combinators

  • Promise.all(arr) — resolves when ALL settle; rejects on first rejection
  • Promise.allSettled(arr) — always resolves with outcomes of all promises
  • Promise.race(arr) — resolves/rejects with whichever settles first
  • Promise.any(arr) — resolves with first fulfillment; rejects if all reject
const [users, products] = await Promise.all([
  fetch('/api/users').then(r => r.json()),
  fetch('/api/products').then(r => r.json())
]); // parallel — much faster than sequential awaits

theory.title: this Keyword & Binding
theory.content:
How this Is Determined

In JavaScript, this is resolved at call time, not definition time (except for arrow functions). Four binding rules, in priority order:

  1. new binding — new Fn() sets this to the freshly created object
  2. Explicit binding — call, apply, or bind override this
  3. Implicit binding — obj.method() sets this to obj
  4. Default binding — standalone call; this is undefined (strict) or global
function greet() {
  return `Hello, ${this.name}`;
}

const user = { name: 'Alice', greet };
user.greet();                   // 'Hello, Alice' — implicit
greet.call({ name: 'Bob' });    // 'Hello, Bob' — explicit

const boundGreet = greet.bind({ name: 'Carol' });
boundGreet();                   // 'Hello, Carol' — bound

Arrow Functions & this

Arrow functions do not have their own this. They capture this from the enclosing lexical scope at definition time — making them ideal for callbacks inside methods.

class Timer {
  constructor() { this.seconds = 0; }

  start() {
    // Arrow captures `this` from start()'s scope (the instance)
    setInterval(() => { this.seconds++; }, 1000);

    // Regular function would lose `this` here:
    // setInterval(function() { this.seconds++; }, 1000); // ERROR
  }
}

Common Pitfalls

  • Passing a method as a callback loses its implicit binding: btn.addEventListener('click', obj.handler) — this becomes the button
  • Fix: obj.handler.bind(obj) or use an arrow wrapper () => obj.handler()
  • In class fields, arrow functions are bound per-instance: handler = () => {...}

theory.title: ES6+ Features
theory.content:
Arrow Functions

Concise syntax for functions, no own this, arguments, or super. Return implicit when body is an expression.

const double = x => x * 2;
const add = (a, b) => a + b;
const getObj = () => ({ key: 'value' }); // wrap object in ()

// Multi-line still needs return
const process = x => {
  const result = x * 2;
  return result + 1;
};

Destructuring

// Objects
const { name, age, role = 'user' } = person; // default value
const { address: { city } } = person;         // nested

// Arrays
const [first, , third] = [1, 2, 3]; // skip element
const [head, ...tail] = arr;         // rest

// In function params
function render({ title, body, className = '' }) { ... }

Spread & Rest

// Spread: unpack into call-site or literal
const merged = { ...defaults, ...overrides };
const copy = [...original, newItem];
Math.max(...numbers);

// Rest: collect remaining args into array
function sum(first, ...rest) {
  return rest.reduce((acc, n) => acc + n, first);
}

Template Literals

const msg = `Hello, ${user.name}! You have ${count} message${count !== 1 ? 's' : ''}.`;

// Tagged templates (advanced)
function highlight(strings, ...values) {
  return strings.reduce((result, str, i) =>
    result + str + (values[i] ? `${values[i]}` : ''), '');
}
const html = highlight`Hello ${name}, you are ${age} years old`;

Optional Chaining & Nullish Coalescing

const city = user?.address?.city;         // undefined if any step is null/undefined
const port = config.port ?? 3000;         // 3000 only if port is null or undefined
const len = arr?.length ?? 0;             // safe length
obj.method?.();                           // call only if method exists

theory.title: Modules (CommonJS vs ES Modules)
theory.content:
CommonJS (CJS)

The original Node.js module system. Modules are loaded synchronously at runtime. The require() call returns the exports object immediately.

// math.js (CJS)
function add(a, b) { return a + b; }
module.exports = { add };
// or: exports.add = add;

// app.js
const { add } = require('./math');
const path = require('path'); // Node built-in
add(1, 2); // 3

ES Modules (ESM)

The official JavaScript standard. Parsed statically before execution — enabling tree-shaking and circular dependency analysis. Use in browsers and Node (with .mjs or "type": "module" in package.json).

// math.mjs (ESM)
export function add(a, b) { return a + b; }
export const PI = 3.14159;
export default class Calculator { ... }

// app.mjs
import Calculator, { add, PI } from './math.mjs';
import * as math from './math.mjs'; // namespace import
import('./heavy-module.mjs').then(m => m.run()); // dynamic import

Key Differences

  • CJS: require is synchronous, can be called conditionally; exports is a plain object that can be mutated
  • ESM: import is static (top-level only), asynchronous; bindings are live — consumers see updates
  • Interop: CJS can be require()-d from ESM via createRequire; ESM default export becomes module.exports in CJS

Dynamic Import

// Code-split lazily — only load when needed
async function loadEditor() {
  const { Editor } = await import('./editor.js');
  return new Editor();
}

// React lazy loading
const LazyPage = React.lazy(() => import('./HeavyPage'));

theory.title: Type Coercion & Equality
theory.content:
Implicit vs Explicit Coercion

JavaScript automatically converts types in many operations (implicit coercion). Understanding the rules prevents subtle bugs.

// String coercion with +
'5' + 3     // '53'  — 3 coerced to string
'5' - 3     // 2     — '5' coerced to number (- has no string meaning)

// Boolean coercion (falsy values)
Boolean(0)          // false
Boolean('')         // false
Boolean(null)       // false
Boolean(undefined)  // false
Boolean(NaN)        // false
// Everything else is truthy, including '0', [], {}

== vs ===

=== (strict equality) checks type AND value — no coercion. Always prefer ===.

0 == false     // true  (both coerce to 0)
'' == false    // true
null == undefined // true (special rule)
null == 0      // false

0 === false    // false (different types)
'' === false   // false

Object Equality

Objects are compared by reference, not by value:

const a = { x: 1 };
const b = { x: 1 };
a === b  // false — different references
a === a  // true  — same reference

// Deep equality: use JSON or a library
JSON.stringify(a) === JSON.stringify(b); // true (fragile)
// Better: lodash isEqual, or structuredClone + ===

typeof & instanceof

typeof 42         // 'number'
typeof 'hello'    // 'string'
typeof undefined  // 'undefined'
typeof null       // 'object' — famous bug, null is NOT an object
typeof []         // 'object'
typeof function(){} // 'function'

[] instanceof Array   // true
[] instanceof Object  // true (arrays inherit from Object)

// Safe null check:
if (value !== null && typeof value === 'object') { ... }
